chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hassan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn al-Sindi from Safwan ibn Yahya from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Abū Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about the zakat of wheat and dates. He said: 'The tenth (ushr) and half the tenth (nisf al-ushr). The tenth is for what is watered by rain, and half the tenth is for what is watered by irrigation.' I said: 'I am not asking you about this; I am asking you about what comes out of it, whether little or much, is there a minimum amount (nisab) from which it is purified?' He said: 'It is purified from what comes out of it, whether little or much: from every ten, one; and from every ten, half one.' I said: 'Are wheat and dates the same?' He said: 'Yes.'

His saying (peace be upon him) at the end of the report: 'It is purified from what comes out of it, whether little or much: from every ten, one; and from every ten, half one.' The meaning is that which exceeds five Awsuq, because that which is less than it does not require zakat. And we will indicate this later. As for the report that he narrated:

key_terms.الْخَمْسَةُ أَوْسَاقٍ: Five Awsuq (a specific volume measure for nisab)

ai.seo_question: What is the minimum amount of wheat or dates subject to zakat in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the zakat rates for wheat and dates are uniform regardless of quantity, provided the harvest exceeds the nisab of five Awsuq. This narration, found in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, establishes the principle that the distinction between rain-watered (one-tenth) and irrigated (half-tenth) crops applies to the rate of deduction rather than the threshold of liability, reinforcing the Shia jurisprudential view on agricultural tithes.
